item.title: UNIT5
item.description:
UNIT 5

When I think of the tech industry, sustainability is never the first thing that comes to my mind. Despite most large tech companies having some sort of ESG framework, it is obvious that these strategies don’t actually serve the environment but instead just server the shareholders. The article that we based our presentation on for this unit covers the details of how little companies actually do help protect our environment while also looking at the issue from a regulatory standpoint.

item.title: UNIT4
item.description:
UNIT 4

This unit consisted of two separate projects where the first involved us creating a dashboard on Metabase and the other task was to create a chatbot.

The Metabase project was challenging in primarily two different aspects: writing SQL queries and figuring out what and how we as a group can present ‌multiple aspects that can be visualized using the data set provided and still make a cohesive story. To find out what each of the dashboards should represent we as a team did some research on what types of charts can be made using the data in the set and then thought of ways to connect different charts to our individual topics and later to make a cohesive group of dashboards. I focused on finding ways of showing the capabilities and limitations of the data set. I am already familiar with Metabase since I have used it before ‌coming to university and I always enjoy using it whenever I have the opportunity.

item.title: UNIT3
item.description:
UNIT 3

I always knew failure was an important part of learning but after reading part of Amy Edmondson’s Right Kind of Wrong, I understood that just failing isn’t enough if we do not understand the type of failure and make it legible to break down and learn from.

The book spoke of three distinct failure types: basic, complex, and intelligent. This was an unfamiliar concept to me. I always looked at failure as a monolithic thing, as Edmondson put it best; something that happens when you aren’t careful enough or not prepared enough. The concept of intelligent failures interested me the most. In the book, Amy talks about an example from her journey into the scientific community where what she initially perceived as a disaster when her research data suggested that better hospital teams made more mistakes instead of the other way around, as intuition might suggest. This “wrong” result, as the prologue explains, was her first intelligent failure. The “failure” didn’t end her career but revealed that high-performing teams felt safe enough to report errors, which led to her discovering psychological safety. This example changed my perspective on how to look at results that don’t justify the thesis of whatever I am working on.

item.title: UNIT2
item.description:
UNIT 2

Unit 2 pushed me to think about information as not just something we consume and have to organise but as something we need to model, transform, and optimise. The classes we had covered a lot of ground (which was overwhelming at times) image transformations, optimisation problems, and the ideas of modelling and abstraction and while some of it was definitely challenging, it was also where things started to come together and fell more concrete.

item.title: UNIT1
item.description:
UNIT 1

Over the first three weeks of the course, we covered wikis, Markdown, and the DIKW model. The lab sessions and theory classes were used to explain how essential wikis are in order to share and democratize information. In the lab we practised Markdown, which is a markup language that allows the writer to format text using readable and simple syntax. The tool we used to write in Markdown is called Zettlr, which is a free to use open-source note-taking platform.
